newsitem.title: USA: Bergsten jitters sends dlr/yen lower by U.S. close.
newsitem.headline: Bergsten jitters sends dlr/yen lower by U.S. close.

text.p: Press speculation the Clinton administration is considering economist Fred Bergsten, a known dollar/yen bear, for a top job in the White House sent the dollar tumbling against the yen Thursday, traders said.

The dollar subsequently hit a session low versus the yen after a large North American money fund, rumored to be that of influencial global investor George Soros, heavily bought yen while selling German marks and Swiss francs.
A spokesman at Soros Funds declined to comment on the market rumor.
An article in the Journal of Commerce newspaper reported Bergsten was in line to replace Laura Tyson to head the National Economic Council.

Bergsten currently heads the Institute for International Economics in Washington and has, in the past, triggered major dollar/yen sell-offs by publically stating the exchange rate should drop below 100.
He previously served in the Treasury Department under President Jimmy Carter.

"The fact is that he's a consummate bear. When that news got out into the market, everyone started to sell dollar/yen fairly hard," said James Powers, vice president in foreign exchange sales and advisory at Westdeutsche Landesbank.
Dollar/yen fell to a low of 111.13, but recovered by the close to end at 111.40/45, below Thursday's open at 111.64/69.

"He's an advocate of using the devaluation of the dollar to try to cure the trade deficit. So the market would view as very suspicious any attempt to try to install him as an advisor to the White House," said Stephen Jury, chief dealer at Union Bank of Switzerland.

Against the mark, the dollar was bolstered by supportive comments from Bundesbank officials, especially President Hans Tietmeyer who said the dollar could go higher and that he welcomes the recent dollar rally.
"The Bundesbank was quite active today in jawboning the dollar higher. When Tietmeyer speaks, that really creates a trading environment," Powers said.
The dollar received a small boost in late trade after Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin reiterated his support for a strong dollar.
Rubin's recent silence regarding dollar policy despite a flurry of comments from other G3 officials had some market players speculating the U.S. stance might change.
The U.S. currency closed higher at 1.5085/95 marks compared to 1.5055/58 marks at Thursday's open.
However, a comment from Bundesbank council member Ernst Welteke halted the dollar's rise against the mark.
Welteke told a news wire he feared Germany and France in 1997 might not meet the budget deficit goals in the Maastricht treaty for a proposed single European currency in 1999.

The dollar held firm against the British pound after hitting its lowest closing level against sterling since October 1992 on Wednesday. Sterling closed at $1.6640/50, slightly weaker than $1.6648/55 at Thursday's open.
In other currencies, the dollar closed at 1.2752/62 Swiss francs and Canadian $1.3353/58, up from 1.2682/87 Swiss francs and C$1.3345/50 at Thursday's open.
The Australian dollar ended at $0.7905/10, down from $0.7915/20 at the open.
-- Roanne Daniels, 212-859-1677
